Abstract
In this thesis we quantify the generation of higher order tones in Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric
Amplifiers (JTWPAs). We discuss the background theory of parametric amplification through optical
non-linear wave mixing. Following this we show a set of experiments in which we observe unexpected
tones. The first experiment describes a resonant device and gives an overview of standard measurement
procedures and an insight into Josephson device behaviour. In the resonant device we demonstrate a
single higher order tone being generated at a frequency which can be mapped back to the three wave
mixing condition. The second experiment involves a more complex travelling wave device. Here we
show that with a single tone one can generate a cascade of higher order harmonics. We then show that
in the case of two input tones one can detect responses at various combinations of sums and differences
of the two tones. This section motivates the rest of the work done in this thesis.
In order to gain insight into our experimental observations we use a circuit simulation software
which includes the Josephson junction circuit element. We confirm the ability to model linear transmis-
sion lines with the software. We then explore the Josephson junction model and produce the standard
results. We then model the travelling wave design which consists of a standard transmission line
embedded with rf SQUIDs. Finally we discuss the observation of higher order tones in the simulation
which are not present in the theory and relate the frequencies of these tones back to the tones observed
in our experiment.
With a focus on these higher order tones we extend the standard coupled mode theory to allow for
these higher order tones to be considered. We also consider the approximations made in the theory and
subsequently alter the simulation to ensure their validity. We then finally resolve any discrepancies
between the simulation and theory. This work forms the principles of my first manuscript which in turn
has led to the further development of ideas to combat such higher order tones

Chapter 1
Introduction
1.1
Motivation
Quantum computing was first envisaged by Richard Feynman in 1982. The proposal was simple, if
a system can be reduced such that quantum states can be differentiated between and manipulated,
then quantum mechanical behaviour can be efficiently simulated. This began the race for a quantum
computer, whose processor would be made of quantum bits (qubits). These are typically two level
systems (TLS), where the considered states of the system are the two lowest energy level states. These
qubits can then be in either of the energy states or any linear superposition of the states. Combining
this with entanglement between qubits would allow for a quantum processor to rapidly outperform a
classical processor comprising of classical bits for certain problems.
Over the last 40 years, a lot of focus was devoted to the development of the qubit. Qubits came
in various forms such as; Superconducting microwave qubits, optical ion trap qubits, semiconductor
quantum dots, and diamond nitrogen vacancy (NV) centres. Each of these have attached pros and cons.
However, at the time of writing this thesis, the first work claiming to demonstrate quantum supremacy
was achieved using superconducting microwave qubits [1].
This “flavour” of superconducting microwave qubits has risen to prominence and is now widely
regarded as the front running technology for a realisable practical quantum computer. From the first
demonstration of superconducting qubits [2] the community has rapidly evolved to overcome many of
the engineering challenges of making, manipulating and measuring these qubits. For the purpose of
this thesis we will solely discuss this superconducting microwave technology and further mention of

17
devices will be based around this type of architecture.
Fundamentally, any useful qubit will always suffer from a near-paradoxical point. In order
to maintain quantum mechanical behaviour, the qubit must be isolated from the highly classical
environment. However to be useful, we as classical entities, must interact with it. This has led to further
development in the wider community. In the same way that a classical computer is more than just a
processor, a practical quantum computer is more than just a qubit. So following this, focus shifted
to further hardware considerations for use in quantum information processing. Of these, low-noise
amplifiers have been quintessential in the reliable measurement of qubits.
Typically superconducting qubits emit photons at the transition energy corresponding to the
difference between the ground and first excited state. For the superconducting qubits these photons are
in the microwave regime f ∼5 GHz and thus have energies of order Ef ≈3.3 × 10−24 J. To aid in
the detection of these the “Josephson Parametric Amplifier” (JPA) has been developed whose noise is
limited by the standard quantum limit [3]. The underlying physics of parametric amplification via the
non-linear response of the Josephson junction is the key phenomena which is studied in this thesis. The
Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier (JTWPA) is a broadband extension of the JPA which
at the time of writing this thesis is the state of the art technology in broadband, low noise amplification
and is the main focus of this thesis.
1.2
Prerequisite Understanding
1.2.1
Non-linear Wave Mixing
Optical Wave Mixing Example
The core principle of parametric amplification derives from the more general phenomenon of Wave
Mixing (WM). This WM phenomenon is typically described by wave equations which contain non-
linear dependencies. The theoretical study of such equations predates the 19th Century [4,5,6]. To
gain an intuition for the origin of parametric amplification deriving from non-linear WM we consider
the phenomenon in terms of an optical WM example [7] and discuss the underlying theory following
the method described in [8].
Optical WM was experimentally recorded in maser technology [7], whereby pulsing an optical

Review
1.3.1
Josephson Parametric Amplifiers
The first mention of JPA measurements was made by H. Zimmer in 1967 [15]. By depositing a thin
strip diagonally across a face on a cube rutile resonator, oxidising in atmosphere for 15 minutes and
then depositing another thin strip at right angles they formed the Josephson junction. This was not
a well controlled procedure and by Zimmer’s own admission “... the formation of a junction in an
evaporated layer is more or less a question a lucky chance...”.
Critically, the junction was known to be a dissipation-less circuit element below its critical current.
With this the attention turned to noise in Josephson circuits. It was known that, by the Heisenberg
uncertainty principle, any bosonic signal must incorporate an uncertainty (S(ω)) of at least S(ω) =
ℏω/2. In 1982, Caves [3], showed that a “phase-insensitive” amplifier must add at least this noise due
to quantum mechanics. However, Caves also showed that this is overcome if one is only interested in
one quadrature phase of the signal. In this case noise can be “squeezed” in the measured quadrature
at the expense of added noise in the unmeasured quadrature. Kuzmin, Likharev, Migulin and Zorin
studied these noise properties directly in the case of JPAs [16]. They found that by operating a JPA in
the degenerate mode, that is where the signal and idler frequency are the same fs = fi, then the added
noise can indeed be lower than the standard quantum limit.
Three years later, in 1985, Smith et. al. [17] specifically measured a JPA in terms of its noise
properties. While a low noise temperature TN ≈6 K was deduced, they also highlighted many of the
sub-optimal properties of the device, which are closely related to this thesis. Firstly, they measured the
device in the three wave mixing (3WM) condition, (fp = fs + fi). Second, they noted the possibility
of other idler frequencies, predominantly the pump harmonic f2p = 2fp or near zero frequency terms,
analysis of these further generated tones form a substantial discussion in this thesis.
Following this, engineering steps were made to optimise the device and in 1989 Yurke measured
both the gain as well as the noise squeezing properties of the JPA [18]. While this demonstration of an
amplifier operating at the fundamental limit of quantum mechanics was novel, practical requirements
for such an amplifier were sparse.
A decade later in 1999 Nakamura, Pashkin and Tsai demonstrated the capability to control the
quantum mechanical states of a two level system (TLS) solid-state device, named the cooper-pair

28
Chapter 1. Introduction
box [2]. This discovery was the first time macroscopic control over the quantum states was shown in
solid-state superconducting devices.
Following this discovery, Wallraff et. al. [19] demonstrated that by embedding such a TLS in
a resonator one can make a continuous transmission measurement by measuring the transmission
properties of the resonator to infer the qubit state. This work led the way for coupling between the
photonic behaviour of qubits to the electrical properties of microwave resonators. Due to the delicate
nature of the measurement previous work in JPAs was revisited. Since JPAs already operate in the
microwave regime, and had been shown to introduce low noise to the system, the community quickly
took to re-purposing these devices in the context of quantum information processing readout tools.
At the same time other single-shot dispersive readout systems were being considered. For example,
Siddiqi et. al. demonstrated a Josephson Bifurcation Amplifier (JBA) [20] which was then used for
single shot qubit readout [21]. Biasing the JJ near a bifurcation point of the system means that an
additional, small, rf-drive can tip the system into one of two distinct oscillation states. These meta-stable
states then apply low back action. Also, by the nature of a bifurcation, these two states are distinct and
stable meaning a latched readout scheme can be achieved. JBAs have been used in qubit readout as
already mentioned as well as platforms for so-called quantum non-demolition measurement [22]. The
latching bifurcation style readout has also been extended to more exotic HyQUID type devices [23] and
Josephson Parametric Oscillators (JPOs) [24,25]. The latter of these also reported single-shot qubit
readout [26] with a fidelity (maximum state discrimination) of 81.5%.
While many of these system demonstrated promising results for single shot readout of a qubit
the community was aware of the scalability of such schemes. The resonant nature of all of these
devices constrained the bandwidth of operation to be within the line-width of the cavity modes. By
utilising two junction Superconducting QUantum Interference Devices (DC SQUIDs) Castellanos-
Beltran and Lehnart [27] were able to tune the resonant mode of a superconducting cavity between
4 −7.8 GHz by applying magnetic flux to adjust the DC SQUID inductance. In this experiment the
JPA was measured over nearly an octave (#octave = log2(fmax/fmin)) of frequencies by adjusting
the magnetic field. They also achieved up to 28 dB gain. The noise temperature TN in the degenerate
case fp = fs = fi ≈6.95 GHz was found to be TN ≈300 mK where the standard quantum limit
noise temperature at this frequency would be ℏω/2kB ≈166 mK, inferring that the input noise of the
amplifier was less than twice the standard quantum limit.

29
As an example of other uses, Hatridge et. al. [28] performed very sensitive magnetometry with
a similar JPA using an embedded DC SQUID to achieve an effective flux noise of 0.14 µΦ0Hz−1/2
over a bandwidth of 0.6 MHz. Returning to qubit readout, Abdo et. al. [29] designed an exotic device
consisting of two perpendicular resonators with four Josephson junctions arranged in a Wheatstone
bridge configuration at the centres (antinodes) of the resonators. Here they achieved modest gain
G > 10 db across an instantaneous bandwidth B ≈60 MHz, and an added photon noise number
of η = 1 ± 0.5 at the signal frequency. This is an example of the implementation of JJs into known
circuitry, such as the Wheatstone bridge to add non-linear wave mixing properties to well understood
circuitry. Still these devices suffered from the gain-bandwidth trade off inherent in resonant devices.
As such, attention turned to travelling wave designs free from the resonator constraints.
1.3.2
Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifiers
Discussions around general travelling wave parametric amplifiers predate the Josephson junction [30].
These devices were called upon for broadband sensitive amplification and again relied upon a non-
linear component to activate the parametric interaction and the wave mixing. These devices were then
reviewed from the point of view of superconducting solid state devices.
Initially, the kinetic inductance of the superconducting film itself provided the non-linearity in so
called Kinetic Inductance Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifiers (KITWPA) [31]. Here, the critical
current of a thin superconducting wire (I∗) gives an upper bound and obvious current scale, much
like the critical current of a JJ (Ic). Well below this critical current one can realise a simple, non-
linear, current dependent result for the kinetic inductance, Lk ≈Lk(0)[1 + (I/I∗)2] [31]. Typically
Lk << LT where LT is the total inductance of the line. This means that the non-linearity is very
weak in the superconducting wire. However using Titanium nitride (TiN) or Niobium-Titanium nitride
(NbTiN) one can increase the normal state resistivity by up to three orders of magnitude [32] which
drastically increases the relative non-linearity of the system.
Such a device was developed and tested by Eom et. al [31]. It was known that harmonic generation
of the pump tone will be the largest generated tone in a bare device. As such, band gap engineering
was utilised by implementing periodic loading along the line. This blocks the generation of the third
harmonic of the pump, and the subsequent cascade of tone generation via waves mixing with this tone.
The coupled mode theory for kinetic inductance devices is very similar to that of Josephson based

30
Chapter 1. Introduction
devices, which are the focus of this thesis.
This coupled mode theory was then extended to include JJs embedded in a transmission line by
Yaakobi et. al. [33]. Here the JJs replace the linear inductor in a standard ladder type transmission
line to form a Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier (JTWPA). With this one can consider
the finite differences between voltage to ground at successive nodes and convert this to flux through
Maxwells equations. In the limit that the unit cell size between nodes is sufficiently smaller than the
wavelength of waves considered these finite differences are converted to a differential wave equation.
These coupled mode equations are discussed in detail in appendix A.2.6.
The theory for JTWPA was then further extended to include resonant phase matching by O’Brien
et. al. [34]. They describe a process whereby simultaneously diminishing the phase matching of
up-converted tones (SFG, harmonic generation) and promoting the phase matching of down-converted
tones (DFG, signal amplification) one can achieve larger and more broadband gain [34]. This is
achieved by capacitively coupling resonators along the line. One can then tune the dispersion relation
of the device such that an asymptotic pole is produced at the resonators frequency. If the pump is then
situated near this frequency, the pump phase can be adjusted, in a tight frequency range, anywhere
between ±π/2. This allows for a linear relationship between pump, signal and idler wave vectors. This
resonant phase matching can also cause a greater phase mismatch in higher frequency tones, reducing
the up-conversion to higher modes.
This idea was developed and tested by T. C. White et. al. [35] in 2015. The device consisted of 1326
JJs in total, separated into 17 sections of 78 JJs each. Each section had a λ/4 resonator capacitively
coupled at its centre. The spacing between resonators was also carefully chosen to be at a spacing
sufficient to suppress third harmonic generation of the pump, as per the band gap engineering in the
KITWPA mentioned previously. However this device only achieved 6 −8 dB of gain. This was then
increased by joining two devices together, however the target 20 dB was not shown.
Shortly after this C. Macklin. et. al. also demonstrated a resonant phase matched JTWPA [36].
This time it consisted of 2037 JJs and 700 resonators spaced every three JJs. This led to considerable
improvements in the gain and bandwidth characteristics, G > 20 dB over a 3 GHz bandwidth. This
coupled with the large bandwidth, high gain and low pump power requirements defined the state-of-the-
art in JTWPA experiments at the start of this project. The main problems with this device were gain
ripples associated with improper impedance matching. Also a pump power dependent phase shift can

1.4
This Thesis
In this thesis we will ultimately look to quantify the generation of higher order tones in Josephson
Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifiers. We provide a background overview to the main phenomena of
nonlinear wave mixing in microwave circuitry. We then show two experiments which highlight the
generation of unwanted higher order modes in such devices. We then move on to SPICE simulations
which further demonstrate the generation of unwanted tones which cascade outside the bandwidth of
our experimental set up. We conclude by developing a numerical model which can account for higher
order tone generation in rf SQUID JTWPAs and demonstrate the accuracy of this model with the circuit
simulation giving insight into the underlying wave mixing mechanisms.
Chapter 2
To highlight the underlying physics, we first discuss the general background theory of parametric
amplification from the point of view of non-linear wave mixing first observed in the optics community.
We discuss how these ideas migrated into the microwave community via the Josephson junction. For
an in-depth understanding of the main topic of this thesis we will analyse two poignant theoretical
papers [14,33]. This will provide all of the background theory necessary to understand the key points
of the rest of the thesis.

1.4. This Thesis
33
Chapter 3
Following this, we show a brief set of experiments. In these experiments we observe the generation of
unwanted higher order tones. We will begin with a resonant based device which will give an overview
of some standard measurement procedures as well as insight into Josephson device behaviour. In the
resonant device we will finally demonstrate a single higher order tone being generated at a frequency
which is mapped back to a three wave mixing condition. We then move on to the more complex
travelling wave device. Here we first show that with just a single tone one can generate a cascade of
higher order harmonic tones. We then show that in the case of two input tones one can detect responses
at various combinations of sums and differences of the two tones. This section motivates the rest of the
work done in this thesis.
Chapter 4
In order to gain insight into our experimental observations, we use a circuit simulation software package,
WRspice, which includes the Josephson Junction circuit element. We first confirm the ability to model
linear transmission lines with the software. We then explore the Josephson junction model and produce
the standard results for single Josephson junctions. We model the theoretical proposal in [14], which
consists of a standard transmission line embedded with rf SQUIDs. Finally, we discuss the observation
of higher order tones in the SPICE simulation which are not present in the current three mode theory
and relate the frequencies of these tones back to the tones observed in our experiment.
Chapter 5
Finally, we focus on these higher order tones, we extend the standard coupled mode theory to allow for
these higher order tones to be considered. We also consider the approximations made in the theory
and subsequently alter the simulation to ensure these approximations are respected. We then finally
resolve the discrepancies between the simulation and theory. This work forms the principles of my
first manuscript [11]. Which has led to the further development of ideas to combat such higher order
tones [39, 40]. We complete this chapter with a brief overview of one such method, quasi-phase
matching. We show through the extended coupled mode theory and circuit simulation that this method
significantly reduces the amplitude of higher order tones, particularly at the output of the quasi-phase

1.4.1
Thesis Statement
To summarise, the aim of this thesis is to resolve many mode interactions in rf SQUID embedded
JTWPAs. We observe these higher order tones both experimentally and through circuit simulation. We
provide an extended numerical model, highlighting the mixing mechanisms and intuition on how these
tones cascade through the device. We demonstrate excellent quantitative agreement between the circuit
simulation and our numerical model. Thus we simultaneously highlight the problem of generation of
unwanted tones, provide a model to explain them and use this understanding to promote engineering
solutions to mitigate this problem.

2.1
Parametric Amplification in Superconducting Circuits
This section will describe the background theory for implementing Josephson junctions into standard
electrical circuitry. First, by looking at a standard transmission line with embedded Josephson junctions
as described by Yaakobi et al. [33], we will see how the non-linear current phase relation enables
wave mixing through a non-linear wave equation. Then we will show how this wave equation may
be modified by replacing the Josephson junction with an rf SQUID as proposed by Zorin [14]. The
introduction of the rf SQUID allows for flux tuning of the device and we will show in detail how
this alters the operating principles of the device. Finally in this section, we will discuss general
considerations one must make when describing practical specifications of such a device.

2.2.1
Control of the Centrosymmetry
A key feature of the rf SQUID JTWPA is the ability to control the strength of β and γ with an external
flux. We calculate these through the transcendental equation eq. (1.29) and plot as per Fig. 2 of [14],
which we have reproduced in fig. 2.3, for a range of SQUID parameters (βL).
Coupling magnetic flux into the rf SQUID loop produces a non-zero phase drop across the junction.
When φDC ̸= 0, sin(φDC) ̸= 0 and thus the even terms in the φAC expansion contribute. This means
the current phase relationship is non-symmetric about its centre, mathematically I(−φAC) ̸= −I(φAC),
or non-centrosymmetric.
From fig. 2.3 and eq. (1.32), we see that maximising the even non-linearity coefficient β (red)
inherently brings γ = 0 (blue) and thus by tuning the DC phase (via tuning the flux threading the
SQUID loop) we tune the contribution of even and odd terms in the expansion.
Typically the language used to describe mixing mechanisms with β = maximum, γ = 0 is “three
wave mixing (3WM)” (non-centrosymmetric) while the γ = maximum, β = 0 coefficient describes
a “four wave mixing (4WM)” mechanism (centrosymmetric). In an unbiased scheme the parametric

Summary
Here, we have discussed in detail the measurement of a resonant device. The simplicity of measuring
within the line width of resonant modes removed much of the frequency dependence from the mea-
surement. Yet there are still complications in describing the mixing processes observed within the
device. These observations led to a consideration of the effects in potential up-conversion to higher
tones in a three wave mixing scheme. We note that off resonance pumping has been demonstrated in
similar devices [48] using three wave mixing however higher order tone generation was not studied.
This higher order tone generation has the potential to hamper device performance in a travelling wave
device, which is free from resonant constraints and allows propagation of tones over a continuous
bandwidth. As such, we now move to experiments with two travelling wave devices where we explore
and demonstrate the generation of these higher order tones.
3.2
Higher Order Tones in Travelling Wave Device
Following from the observation of potential up conversion in resonant devices, we also measure two
travelling wave devices sent from partners at Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) named
JTWPA1 and JTWPA2. These devices consist of N ≈1000 rf SQUIDs embedded in a co-planar
wave-guide transmission line. The devices are first and second generation travelling wave parametric
amplifiers respectively. For this thesis, we focus on the observation of higher order tone generation and
how this can hamper parametric amplification. The most dominant tone generation is suspected to be
pump harmonics. As such, we first discuss the case of a single input tone, the pump tone, and how that
generates harmonics. We then look at two input tones, pump and signal, and how a myriad of tones are
generated from these.

characteristics were non-optimal and so I was tasked with understanding what may be affecting
amplifier performance. One of the main concerns was harmonic generation of the pump tone. To
measure just the cascaded pump harmonic generation we insert one tone, assigned as the pump tone.

3.3
Summary
We have made a number of experimental observations that show the existence of tones which are
not considered in the standard treatment of parametric amplifiers. First, we showed in a resonant
based device that we could explain the existence of a tone situated at the third mode of the resonator
through an up conversion three wave mixing process. We then showed in a more complex device and
experimental set up that these tones may be generated in travelling wave parametric amplifiers. It is
these observations that motivate the rest of the thesis, where we analyse the generation of higher order
tones in more detail.

To aid in understanding what may be happening inside the device we have used a SPICE-like circuit
simulator, WRspice, to model the device. “Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis”
(SPICE) software originated from Berkeley and is widely used for detailed modelling of electrical
systems. The model is a lumped element circuit model made by defining a “netlist” circuit file and
passing it to the simulator.
Recently WRspice [50], a SPICE package which includes the Josephson junction (JJ) circuit
element, became recently available as open-source. The JJ model is extensive and details of which
can be found online or printed from the full manual. One key realisation of the following work
was the ability to create netlists (circuit files) in MATLAB and be able to pipe (pass) them via the
terminal (cmd line in Windows) to WRspice allowing for simulations to be scaled up with the aid of
high-performance cluster based parallel processes. To do this the MINERVA High Performance Cluster
(HPC) at Cambridge University was used.
In this section, we will show first that we can accurately model linear transmission lines as discussed
in section 1.2.2. We will then show the ability to accurately describe the Josephson junction (JJ) as
discussed in section 1.2.3. Finally, we will combine all of this to build up to a model of the rf SQUID
embedded Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier (JTWPA). We will centre this entire section
around circuit parameters given in appendix A.2.4 for ease of discussion.

The introduction of the AC pump and signal shifts the junction phase, causing time dependence in
the junction contribution. This is what allows the non-linear behaviour and the wave mixing, but may
also modify the impedance and dispersion of the line by modulating the Josephson inductance, and
causing possible reflections. It is worth noting that the most severe reflections will happen at either end
of the device where the termination resistors are mismatched to the end rf SQUID impedance. “Front
end” reflections are typically referred to as a source of insertion loss, this affects the input current to
the device. While “back end” reflections are referred to as back action and the reflected backward
travelling waves may interfere with forward travelling waves within the device and set up standing
wave interference.
It is also worth noting that the impedance of the line is frequency dependent and thus can never be
perfectly matched for all rf tones, and so even in a device with no phase oscillations, perfect impedance
matching is impossible for any more than 1 input tone.

4.5
Summary
We have shown in this section that WRspice is able to accurately model simple transmission lines
through a lumped element analysis. Furthermore, we have touched upon other practical considerations
such as frequency dependent insertion loss and impedance mismatch which are not routinely discussed
in the current literature. We have then shown how this is modified with the inclusion of a linear
shunt capacitor to increase the dispersion curvature and reduce the cut-off frequency, again WRspice
replicates the result of standard lumped element theory.

Chapter 5
Resolving WRspice Simulation and
Theory
Thus far we have shown, through simulation and experiment, that higher order tones exist in rf
SQUID embedded Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifiers (JTWPAs). Previous theories
describe an interaction of three tones, namely the pump, signal and idler. This model in the undepleted
pump case relied solely on the Difference Frequency Generation (DFG) of pump and signal(idler)
to generate(amplify) the idler(signal) tone. We have seen experimentally that higher order tones of
Sum Frequency generation (SFG) and Harmonic Generation (HG) are observed in devices. We have
then further showed that in a SPICE circuit simulator these tones cascade upwards through three wave
mixing (3WM) mechanisms to frequencies which would be difficult to measure with off the shelf
microwave circuitry.
What we would like to do is resolve the differences between the observations we have made in
previous chapters with a theory which is extended from the standard treatment to many tones. To do
this, we first want to see if we can reduce the complexity of the behaviour seen in the simulation. We
then consider the implication of orders of interaction and how this cascades throughout the device. Then
finally, we look to develop a theory which considers a logical set of frequencies defined by properties
of the device which quantitatively compare to simulation results.

5.1
Controlling the WRspice Simulation
Firstly, it is understood that the simulation and the CME theory will not completely agree. The
simulation includes things highlighted previously such as insertion loss, internal reflections and higher
order corrections. Also within the simulation changes in parameters are dynamic such as the phase on
the junction φ ∝arccos−1(LJ) which modifies the junction contribution to the total inductance as per
eq. (A.23). The simulations are akin to a black box theory, where we insert the inputs, crank the handle
and plot the outputs.
WRspice benefits from an extensive manual outlining the simulation procedure. However we
still confirm the results of the simulations with a theory derived from physical principles, such as
the coupled mode theory. In order to do so it is worth examining the CMEs and understanding the
assumptions made within the theory to see if we can bring the two models into a better agreement.
One assumption made was that the junction phase is set to π/2 and remains at this position such
that the inductive path through the junction is infinite, and thus the total inductance is defined by the
geometric inductance, eq. (A.23). Similarly the expansion of the rf SQUID current-phase relationship
(CPR) in eq. (1.32) relies on a small AC variation in the junction phase. In fact, from eq. (1.32) we
see that if the DC phase component φDC strays from π/2 then the odd terms in the expansion become
non-zero, while for larger AC oscillations of φ then the approximation becomes less accurate. In
WRspice, we are able to measure the phase drop across the junction with the use of a third node Bx

Summary
In the previous sections of this chapter we have shown that by lowering both the pump and signal input
power then we can reduce the phase oscillations over the junction. The small angle approximation in
the CME theory requires that the phase shift around the DC bias point is small and for the lower power
regime we show that this assumption is now met. In reducing the power we have also seen more clearly
the preferential mixing mechanism of pump second harmonic generation. This mixing mechanism
draws energy from the pump and as a result reduces the signal amplification. We then further showed
that the cascade of harmonic generation may still be via three wave mixing, i.e still apparent in the low
power regime for small AC oscillations. This discovery forms the motivation for the key results in this
thesis and that is being able to quantitatively describe the generation of these higher order modes.

If we examine the labelled terms we get a deeper understanding of the mixing mechanisms present
within the device:
(i) This term shows that the SFG mixing of the signal and idler then generates a tone at the pump
frequency. This allows for a more general theory beyond the strong pump approximation. This
has been shown in [14], as well as previously in our three tone model and is responsible for
energy flow back and forth the pump and signal/idler tones.
(ii) This term shows that the DFG mixing of the signal and idler then generates a tone at the
difference of the two frequencies fδ. Conveniently, up until now, we have considered a signal
with a frequency fs = (3/5)fp. This means that through the 3WM condition fi = (2/5)fp and
thus fδ = (1/5)fp and that any combination of any tone considered through any further mixing
will always be a multiple of fδ. As such, there will not be a tone with a frequency lower than
fδ. To be complete; if the signal had been some irrational fraction of the pump, then an infinite
number of smaller frequency tones may be generated through cascaded difference frequency
generation.
(iii) These two terms show how a tone at fp+δ = (6/5)fp is generated through either (a) DFG
between the (pump + signal) and (idler), fp+s −fi = fδ tone or, (b) SHG of the signal fs + fs.

106
Chapter 5. Resolving WRspice Simulation and Theory
Note that both of these mechanisms involve no pump or pump harmonic tone and thus are not
pump mediated. By considering only pump mediated mixing (at least one tone being at the
pump or pump harmonic) we avoid an infinite number of frequencies cascading downward in
frequency, even for irrational ratios of fs/fp.
(iv) This term shows that the SFG of the pump and its own second harmonic generates a tone at the
third harmonic of the pump frequency. This is an SFG term in the 3WM case (as opposed to
THG in the 4WM regime). In the 3WM case, the coefficient of HG has a factor 1/2 which is
understood from the coefficients described by Pascal’s triangle, which is true for every order of
wave mixing.
(v) This term shows that the HG of the second harmonic of the pump generates a tone that is now at
f4p. This highlights the fact that there must be some upper bound placed on the frequencies we
consider to avoid an infinite number of frequencies cascading upward in frequency.
Here, we have highlighted the ideas behind a brute force extension to the CMEs used in section 2.2.2.
Through this method we have found that it is possible to create an infinite number of tones at frequencies
lower and higher than those previously considered.
Infinitely many, lower frequency tone generation, comes from the potential for cascaded DFG
between signal and idler tones, for signal frequencies which are some irrational ratio of the pump tone.
This is counteracted by considering only pump mediated tones, and as such, discarding any mixing
between just signal and idler such that fδ and its associated mixing products never proliferate through
the maths.
Infinitely many higher frequency tones, may be generated from the cascaded SFG and HG of tones.
This is counteracted by applying an upper limit on the maximum frequency considered, which may be
taken from simulation or theoretical models specific for each device.

5.3. Extension to Coupled Mode Theory
113
Using an extension to the CMEs in comparison to the WRspice output we are able to explain and
understand the complete behaviour of our simulated device. We have given an explicit example of
an extension to the coupled mode equations. The brute force extension gives rise to additional tones
oscillating at various sums and differences of both the initially input tones (pump and signal) as well as
the cascade of generated tones (every other tone). This cascade of generated tones is produced in the
3WM condition, in contrast to a higher order power expansion of the Josephson relation, and thus is
still feasible in the low power limit. However, this technique is extendable to arbitrary higher order
wave mixing conditions (4WM, 5WM, ...), where only the frequency mixing conditions for each wave
mixing scenario would need to be revised. While we have purposefully moved to a lower input power
regime, which reduces the erratic behaviour of the device, we still see more complex behaviour than
initially thought. The higher order tone generation cascades through the device and interacts with each
other. In the CME-5 case there are 121 mixing mechanisms considered, compared to 3 in CME-1.
Furthermore for brevity and pedagogical reasons we have not included the non-pump-mediated case,
but we would expect that the fit may be improved further by including these tones. As a final message,
we show in fig. 5.15 the possible issue of not including an extended CME theory when analysing the
signal propagation and gain.
Figure 5.15 shows that if one was to model the circuit through CME-1 and neglect higher order terms
then the JTWPA would be fabricated to be 1250 nodes long, fig. 5.15a) (blue solid line) such that the sig-
nal was maximised at the output. The gain from CME-1 at this node is GCME−1(1250) ≈24 dB. How-
ever, the WRspice result in fig. 5.15b) shows that this gain would be closer to GWRspice(1250)10.3 dB,
less than half that expected. In fact, through each sequential extension of the CMEs we see that the
fit of the entire signal profile along the device is improved by each extension. By understanding the
interactions of higher order tones within the extended theory, which has been verified by WRspice
simulations, we may then look for potential solutions to suppress such interactions. Furthermore, we
intend to develop this extended theory to include arbitrarily many tones by exploring symmetries in the
brute force extension to the coupled mode equations.

Refining this work could open many possibilities to further understanding the complex behaviour in
these devices. Firstly one is not necessarily limited to just a pump and signal input tone. If broadband
amplification is required to detect multiple signals then it stands to reason that these signals may be
input at the same time and different frequencies in the device. There is no immediately obvious reason
why this could not be considered with this type of analysis by a) giving multiple input signals at the first
step, b) then providing these input signals with a non-zero initial value in the ODE solver. Secondly
one can extend this method to any other higher order mixing mechanism and thus potentially describe
higher power 5WM, 7WM, ... mechanisms and try to understand the features at high powers in the
device. Also there is no reason why at each iteration one could not describe a mixed mixing state of
3WM and 4WM simultaneously. One could input the pump and signal, perform the first 3WM iteration
and collect the frequencies generated. Then with those frequencies perform the first 4WM iteration
and collect those frequencies. repeating this step would lead to two mixing matrices representing each
mixing condition. But then by simply collecting all of the same frequency mixing mechanisms from
both matrices and applying the individual coefficients one produces a mixed 3WM and 4WM which
may be useful for analysing devices which are at a mixed bias position, see fig. 2.3. Similarly any
dispersion engineering is incorporated by adjusting the dispersion relationship used and subsequently
the k(ω) entered into the CMEs. We believe there is a great deal of further application for this numerical
approach to understand the complex behaviour of these devices.

Recently, Zorin proposed a method that could mitigate the generation of unwanted tones by using
a technique referred to as Quasi Phase Matching (QPM) [39]. This technique has been used within

introduces functions by the method of periodic poling [57]. As the wavelength of the tones are much

5.5
Summary
We have shown that by lowering the input power to the rf SQUID JTWPA, we move away from an
erratic regime.
In this lower power regime the cascade of three wave mixing mechanisms became more clear and
we were able to develop an extension to the CME theory. We did this by considering all of the possible
generated frequencies based on an iteration of the three wave mixing condition. By doing this, we
showed that even in the small signal limit the cascaded effect of the presence of higher order tones

5.5. Summary
127
allowed for many higher frequencies to be analysed.
We showed that by considering these tones, we produce a very good fit for a complex system
over all tones as showed in fig. 5.14. Furthermore, we highlight to the community the dangers of not
including such tones and showed in fig. 5.15 how this may manifest in a reduction in the expected gain
at the output of a device.
Finally, we have briefly discussed on the idea of Quasi Phase Matching as suggested in [39]. This
is a recent proposal, and the analysis we show in section 5.4 gives a hopeful outlook on the idea. The
tools and understanding developed in this section have proven valuable resources to verify and optimise
such proposals and in fig. 5.25 we show a device achieving G < 20dB

Chapter 6
Conclusion
6.1
Conclusion
In this thesis, I have focused on the development of a robust, practical amplifier designed for the
microwave regime, and in particular as the first stage in a chain of amplifiers targeted at quantum
information processing.
Essential requirements of such a device were; gain, G ≈20 dB over an instantaneous bandwidth
4 −8 GHz. Through measurement of partner devices and simulation of the design proposed by
Zorin [14], I discovered that broadband devices are more complex then their resonant counterparts. As
such, we refocused our efforts in to understanding this more complex behaviour outlined in chapter 4
and chapter 5 which resulted in publication [11]. These models have given us extensive insight into
previously unexpected behaviour.
In our experiments, we first show up-conversion to higher modes in devices constrained to operate
within resonant frequency conditions. The realisation of this led to the initial concern of up-conversion
in devices which have a large bandwidth of operation.
We then show the effect of cascaded harmonic generation in such a travelling wave device. We
show SHG at the three wave mixing (3WM) bias point, and THG at the four wave mixing (4WM) and
3WM bias point - THG in the 3WM demonstrates cascaded harmonic generation in JTWPAs. We also
show the Sum Frequency Generation within a travelling wave device and show that these tones can
grow larger than the idler, meaning they can no longer be neglected in the analysis of such a device.
I have extended the analytical model of three mode interactions for parametric amplification to
128

6.1. Conclusion
129
include higher order mixing processes. By solving this numerically, we can quantify the higher order
effects and their implications for the total system, including detrimental effects on signal gain in
broadband parametric amplifiers. To highlight this, we demonstrate their effects in a simulated JTWPA
and compare numerical results with simulation. It is important to consider both of these methods. The
analytic model gives functional dependencies which can help understand how the device responds to
changes in parameters. While the numerical model allows for exploration of any assumptions made in
deriving an analytic result.
In addition, we show that tools such as WRspice provide a more complete simulation than analytic
or numerical solution of CME’s can provide. We also note that WRspice has the capability to include
device parameter spreads important for devices with extensive fabrication complexity such as the
JTWPAs discussed, this is useful when evaluating experimental results. Ultimately, by understanding
the mechanisms driving these higher order tones we can then look to develop devices which counteract
the generation of unwanted tones.
One such recent development was proposed at the time of writing this thesis by Zorin [39], by
using quasi-phase matching (QPM) one can simultaneously combat up-conversion tones and promote
signal amplification. By using our extended theory we first corroborate that QPM reinforces signal gain
along the line. Also, we can demonstrate by including higher order terms that QPM actively disrupts
up-conversion to the sum frequency fp+s,i and pump second harmonic f2p; thus inhibiting the cascade
of higher order tone generation.
We then show, in WRspice, that while the signal growth does exponentially increases along the line
there are a number of considerations that must be made when comparing with theory; such as phase
stability, and pump power limitations.
Finally, we provide device parameters and optimal working points based on current technologies
with which we believe a QPM-JTWPA can achieve high-gain. We conclude that this type of engineering
which targets the core pump-signal interaction (high-gain), while broadly disrupting higher order
loss mechanisms (broad-band), provides an exciting new development for practical small-signal
amplification.

130
Chapter 6. Conclusion
6.2
Further Work
The most pressing work is the fabrication and measurement of the rf SQUID embedded JTWPA. While
in this thesis the simulation and extension of the CME’s has shown the device may require further
engineering it is feasible that a longer (n > 2500) JTWPA may still achieve modest gain (G > 10 dB)
over a large (4 −8 GHz) bandwidth. Further optimising this design through standard engineering
techniques may yield greater gain figures and coupled with the tunability of the rf SQUID JTWPA this
may still prove vital to the community.
We expect that work on fabricating and measuring a Quasi-phase matched JTWPA to demonstrate
the proposal in [39] would yield an interesting and novel approach to increasing the performance of the
rf SQUID JTWPA. Also this approach may be used to suppress specific frequencies and as such may
be used for the specific elimination of unwanted tones. By comparing experimental results with circuit
simulations we can further verify the accuracy of our simulation and this would allow us to further
optimise designs.
We also note that the WRspice tool allows for simulation of variation of design parameters to be
easily modelled. This work has been undertaken by collaborators and the results made available via
a pre-print on the arXiv [58]. This will give more information to the community, particularly in the
design and fabrication stages of JTWPA development.
In the experiment section we noted the observation of tones spontaneously generated inside
modes of the pumped resonator. This observation is not fully understood however such instances of
spontaneous tone generation have been noted previously [59]. More recently other collaborators have
measured a similar sample and demonstrated a number of tones being generated through stimulated
wave mixing (where both pump and signal are introduced) [60]. It would be interesting to explore these
devices further to map out the regimes of both stimulated wave mixing and spontaneous emission of
tones. These may be useful for on chip tone generation in future experiments.
We also note that the generation of tones in broadband devices may be useful for certain applications.
The JTWPA has already been theoretically proposed as a squeezed state generator [61,62]. However
if a general quantum theory can be derived which maps to the extended coupled mode equations
given here then we may expect the ability to generate multiple entangled states over a large frequency
spectrum. Coupling this with the QPM engineering and tunabilty of the rf SQUID, one might propose a

B.2
WRspice Netlist
The WRspice netlist is a list of circuit elements which is then parsed to the WRspice program via
MATLAB. The .txt file is generated programatically to allow for iterative unit cells to be quickly written
to the .txt file. The junction model is defined on line 3 to have zero shunt resistance, a critical current
Ic = 5 µA, and a junction capacitance CJ = 60 fF. The pump and signal current sources are then
defined on lines 4, 5 with the phase offset, amplitude, frequency, time delay respectively. Next we
define the front end resistor with ammeters either side on lines 7, 6, 8. This is then followed by a long
list of the rf SQUID array. Following the rf SQUID netlist we include the termination resistor. This
defines the circuit however the bottom 4 lines also describe some simulation parameters. The time
step is controlled by the “.tran” line, where the time step dt = 1 ps, total time ttot = 30 ns, wait
time tdelay = 0 are defined. The time vector can also be returned from the simulation which aids in the
Fourier analysis. The uic condition tells the simulator to use any initial conditions provided which in
this example are not given. We also set the maxdata property to 8e8 as many timesteps on many
nodes can produce a lot of data.

Capturing Complex Behaviour in Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric Ampliﬁers
T. Dixon,1, 2 J. W. Dunstan,2 G. B. Long,1 J. M. Williams,1 P. J. Meeson,2 and C. D. Shelly1, ∗
1National Physical Laboratory, Hampton Road, Teddington, TW11 0LW, United Kingdom
2Royal Holloway University of London, Egham, Surrey, TW20 0EX, United Kingdom
(Dated: December 12, 2019)
We present an analysis of wave-mixing in recently developed Josephson Travelling Wave Paramet-
ric Ampliﬁers (JTWPAs). Circuit simulations performed using WRspice show the full behaviour of
the JTWPA allowing propagation of all tones. The Coupled Mode Equations (CMEs) containing
only pump, signal, and idler propagation are shown to be insuﬃcient to completely capture complex
mixing behaviour in the JTWPA. Extension of the CMEs through additional state vectors in the
analytic solutions allows closer agreement with WRspice. We consider an ordered framework for the
systematic inclusion of extended eigenmodes and make a qualitative comparison with WRspice at
each step. The agreement between the two methods validates both approaches and provides insight
into the operation of the JTWPA. We show that care should be taken when using the CMEs and
propose that WRspice should be used as a design tool for non-linear superconducting circuits such
as the JTWPA.
I.
INTRODUCTION
A.
Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric
Ampliﬁers
Josephson junction (JJ) based parametric ampliﬁers
(JPAs) [1–3] have been used in recent years to pro-
vide quantum-limited noise performance for quantum op-
tics experiments [4], single microwave photon detection
[5], high-ﬁdelity qubit readout for quantum information
technologies [6, 7], as well as producing squeezed states
[8]. These microwave, small signal, ampliﬁers have been
shown to exhibit large gain (> 20 dB) [9, 10], and ap-
proach the quantum noise limit [11]. Typically these am-
pliﬁers have utilised high-Q superconducting resonators
which have a limited bandwidth and dynamic range.
Removing the resonant architecture and allowing non-
linear interactions along a transmission line can increase
both the dynamic range and bandwidth [12]. More re-
cently, the Josephson Travelling Wave Parametric Am-
pliﬁer (JTWPA), based on JJs embedded in a microwave
transmission line has been shown to provide large gain
without the bandwidth limitation of the JPAs [13–15].
Implementing unbiased JJs along the transmission line
leads to a centrosymmetry of the system and four wave
mixing (4WM) whereby the signal and idler frequencies
are close to the frequency of the pump, fs + fi = 2fp.
In this paper we focus primarily on the three wave mix-
ing (3WM) scheme, fs + fi = fp which shifts the pump
frequency away from that of the signal and idler allow-
ing the pump to be ﬁltered more easily from the sig-
nal. The 3WM regime also takes advantage of the in-
herently stronger interactions than the 4WM regime. In
this regime the phase modulation eﬀect and the signal
gain are controlled independently, the process of which
is described in detail by Zorin [16]. To access the 3WM

II.
MODELLING THE JTWPA
A.
WRspice Simulations
In order to capture the full behaviour of the JTWPA,
we use WRspice to simulate the circuit design shown in
Fig. 1. WRspice is a SPICE-like circuit simulator which
includes a Josephson junction model [17]. Conventional
analytical models describing three-wave mixers consider
only three mixing tones, the pump fp, signal fs, and idler
fi [18].
Using WRspice we observe that other mixing
tones, especially the harmonics of the pump, are gener-

III.
DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
Our extension of the CMEs show that CME-1 (includ-
ing only the pump, signal, and idler) is insuﬃcient to
capture the complex behaviour of the JTWPA. As we
increase the number of terms in the CMEs we approach
the behaviour and gain ﬁgures observed in WRspice sim-

6
ulations. We note that whilst good agreement between
CME-5 and WRspice is achieved, there is still not full
agreement. We now speculate below on the sources of
the remaining discrepancy.
Only the quadratic term in the current-phase relation
of the ﬂux-biased SQUID is included in the formation
of the CMEs. Inclusion of the quartic (and higher-order)
terms may bring the WRspice and CME results into even
better agreement. The dc oﬀset generated by all other
tones (optical rectiﬁcation) is also not included in the
CMEs whilst a dc current is seen in the WRspice for high
pump currents. Finally, our choice of CME extensions are
based on the WRspice results which show large amplitude
pump harmonic and pump-mediated tones. Only these
tones are included in the CME extensions we have pre-
sented in this work. Additional tones, including higher
harmonics of the signal, may need consideration for im-
proved agreement between WRspice and the CMEs.
We believe these results will have practical conse-
quences for the design and operation of JTWPAs, in
particular for considerations of measurement bandwidth,
tone reﬂections, and optimisation procedures.
To conclude, we demonstrate that a simple consider-
ation of only three tones is insuﬃcient to describe the
complex behaviour of the JTWPA. We have presented
four further extensions of the coupled mode equations,
increasing the number of interacting tones included with
each extension. We also used WRspice to simulate the
JTWPA and compared its output to that of the extended
coupled mode equations. Each further extension of the
CMEs agreed more accurately with the WRspice simula-
tion.
We note that whilst good agreement between CME-5
and WRspice is achieved, there is still not full agreement
and we have discussed possible reasons for this. In or-
der to design an ampliﬁer, and to obtain representative
gain ﬁgures all of the behaviour of the JTWPA should
be included. In this regard WRspice should be consid-
ered as the most reliable design tool.
Both the simu-
lations and the extended CME analytical theory show
clearly that the generation of pump harmonics and the
pump-mediated sum frequency generation terms must be
considered when designing such a broadband device. In
order to achieve the gains required for a usable JTWPA
suﬃcient for quantum-limited ampliﬁcation, engineering
to suppress the pump harmonic generation may need be
implemented. Some of this engineering is already consid-
ered in the form of stop-band engineering [14, 16, 20].
This work realises a simple, computationally inexpen-
sive, method for extension of the CMEs describing propa-
gators which have been previously neglected and demon-
strates the utility of WRspice for simulation of non-linear
superconducting circuits, in particular as a design tool for
JTWPAs.

We numerically investigate the behavior of a Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifier assuming a
current-phase relation with a second–harmonic contribution. We find that varying the weight of harmonic
terms in the Josephson current affects the gain profile.
The analysis of gain characteristics, phase-space
portraits, Poincar´e sections, and Fourier spectra demonstrates that the nonsinusoidal contribution influences
the operating mode and stability of the device. In particular, we identify the optimal weighting of harmonic
contributions that maximizes amplification, achieving gains up to ∼13 dB in a device without dispersion
engineering.
Boosting weak microwave signals is essential in many
application fields, like reading superconducting qubits,
quantum devices, and radio astronomy1–3. Optimal low-
noise microwave amplifiers get close to the quantum–
noise limit by working at very low temperatures and
using parametric pumping in circuits with Josephson
junctions (JJs) or superconducting elements with high
kinetic inductance4.
Superconducting
amplifiers
based
on
nonlinear
resonators usually have reasonable gain and quantum-
limited noise,
but feature a limited bandwidth of
a few hundred MHz.
Alternatively,
the so-called
traveling-wave
parametric
amplifiers
(TWPAs)
can
achieve much wider bandwidths, up to several GHz5–7.
This aspect is especially useful for reading multiple
qubits and detection applications8. The efficient use of
quantum hardware through frequency multiplexing is a
crucial factor for the scalability of quantum processors.
However, superconducting TWPAs have also drawbacks,
such as gain ripples, generation of unwanted tones and
comparatively lower gain. These challenges need to be
addressed by proper design of the distributed amplifiers
and control of the intrinsic nonlinearities.
Superconducting
TWPAs
are
currently
realized
using the high nonlinear kinetic inductance found in

In the latter case they are called

One of the
primary goals in designing a JTWPA is determining
strategies that maximize signal amplification,
while
keeping a good control of the system bandwidth and
of spurious tones generation.
The amplifier’s gain
can be optimized through dispersion engineering, e.g.,
by resonant phase matching strategies19–21 involving
periodically
embedded
LC
resonators
capacitively
coupled to the transmission line: the resonators adapt
the dispersion relation so that the total phase mismatch
along the transmission line remains small over a wide
bandwidth.
Other dispersion–engineering strategies
to maximize the achievable gain and the robustness
of the device response can be also implemented22–27.
The basic element of a JTWPA, i.e., the Josephson
junction, determines the device performance.
Usually,
a JJ is assumed to follow a sinusoidal current-phase
relation (CPR). However, this is not always the case,
as higher harmonics are often observed in the CPR of
unconventional JJs28,29.
For instance, in nanobridge-
based junctions, deviations from a sinusoidal CPR at
high temperatures to a sawtooth-like or even multivalued
form at lower temperatures arise due to phase slippage
effects in the weak link30. In this work, we precisely focus
on the gain profiles in the specific case of a CPR with a
second–harmonic contribution.
To do so, we numerically investigate the behavior of a
JTWPA31,32 with the realistic system parameter setting
from the design developed within the DARTWARS
INFN collaboration8,33–39.
In particular, we consider

In summary, we have numerically studied the behavior
of a JTWPA formed by junctions with a CPR that
includes a second–harmonic contribution.
The results
show that, by adjusting the balance between the weights
of the CPR harmonic components, it is possible to
achieve a significant amplification, with gains up to ∼
13 dB, even in the absence of dispersion engineering.
Additionally,
we have observed how non–sinusoidal
contributions in the CPR can lead to a transition
from stable, periodic behavior to chaotic dynamics,
particularly for Jc2 < 0.
These findings highlight the
potential for optimizing JTWPA performance through
the careful tuning of the harmonic components, offering
an additional avenue for improving amplifier designs.

Properties of Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric
Ampliﬁer With a Non-Sinusoidal Current-Phase
Relation and Resonant Phase Matching
Claudio Guarcello
, Carlo Barone
, Giovanni Carapella
, Giovanni Filatrella
, Andrea Giachero
,
and Sergio Pagano
Abstract—A comprehensive numerical analysis of the dynami-
cal response of Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Ampliﬁers
(JTWPA) under varying driving conditions is presented. The pri-
mary goal is to examine the effects of a current–phase relation
(CPR) incorporating a second-harmonic contribution. The analysis
further investigates how parameters such as pump intensity, signal
frequency, and DC bias current inﬂuence the transition to chaos.
The results reveal a wide range of dynamical regimes in JTWPAs,
offering insights into optimizing device performance and stability.
Notably, the shape of the CPR is shown to have a signiﬁcant
impact on the operational effectiveness and stability of JTWPAs.
To obtain results closer to real devices, numerical modeling of
JTWPAs implementing Resonant Phase Matching (RPM) circuitry
has been performed. We have veriﬁed that the introduction of RPM
allows a signiﬁcant increase in the ampliﬁer gain also in the case
of non-sinusoidal CPR. These ﬁndings may have important impli-
cations for the development of next-generation JTWPAs, which
are essential components in quantum computing and precision
measurement applications.
Index Terms—Josephson junctions, parametric ampliﬁers,
quantum-noise limited ampliﬁers, superconducting microwave
devices.

I. INTRODUCTION
A
MPLIFYING weak microwave signals for the readout of
superconducting qubits or for interfacing quantum detec-
tors is essential for applications in quantum computing, basic
physics experiments, and radio astronomy. The best low-noise
microwave ampliﬁers reach the quantum-noise limit by work-
ing at very low temperatures and using parametric pumping
in circuits with Josephson junctions (JJs) or superconducting
elements with high kinetic inductance [1]. Among supercon-
ducting parametric ampliﬁers, Josephson Traveling Wave Para-
metric Ampliﬁers (JTWPAs) offer large bandwidth, high gain,
and high saturation power, at the expense of a rather complex
structure with many elements [2], [3], [4], [5], [6]. This com-
plexity may result in unwanted effects, such as signal reﬂection,
oscillation, spurious harmonic generation, and even chaotic
behavior [7].
Proper modelling of the dynamical system forming a
JTWPA, without simplifying approximations is, therefore, a
crucial aspect. Moreover, as parametric ampliﬁers increas-
ingly rely on unconventional weak links with high trans-
parency, and hence non-sinusoidal current–phase relations
(CPRs), [8] it becomes important to develop JTWPA descrip-
tions that capture CPR harmonics and their impact on the device
nonlinearity.
II. THE JOSEPHSON TRAVELING WAVE PARAMETRIC
AMPLIFIER
A JTWPA is a transmission line composed of many cells,
each containing one or more JJs, the nonlinear elements. Among
the various possibilities, we focused on a cell made of a loop
formed by a JJ and a superconducting inductor (forming an RF-
SQUID cell), and with a capacitor to ground, see Fig. 1. The JJ
is modeled, following the standard Resistively Shunted Junction
(RSJ) model, as the parallel combination of a “pure” Josephson
element, a capacitor C J and a resistor R J (here we used R J =
20 kΩ) [9], [10], [11]. The current ﬂowing through and voltage
across each JJ are then given by:

The different CPR can be a result of the materials forming

[14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]. Normally, a “standard”, i.e.,
sinusoidal, CPR is used to model a JTWPA. However, as more
research is done in improving the device performances, the
presence of a nonstandard CPR cannot be excluded. JTWPAs
made with junctions having a CPR with variable transparency
have been investigated in [20], where it is found that the device
response is highly sensitive to the speciﬁc form of the CPR.
Increasing its skewness leads to a reduction of the maximum
achievable gain, while at the same time enlarging the range
of pump intensities over which the system remains stable.
Moreover, the onset of chaotic dynamics becomes considerably
sharper at higher skewness.
A second-harmonic CPR has been shown to accurately de-
scribe superconducting junctions with ferromagnetic barriers
[17], [21], as well as JJs based on semiconductors [22], [23],
[24], [25], graphene [26], and unconventional superconductors
[27], [28]. Although higher-harmonic contributions are typically
negligible in conventional tunnel junctions, recent work has
demonstrated that they can also modify the excited-state spec-
trum of Al- and AlO-based Josephson qubits [29]. Relatedly,
microscopic barrier inhomogeneities (e.g., pinholes or weak
points) can yield a small set of highly transmissive channels
and thereby enhance higher-harmonic contributions even in
nominally Al/AlO x
/Al tunnel junctions [30], [31]. Finally,
we note a recent mesoscopic theory for JJs formulated within
nonrelativisticscalarelectrodynamics,inwhichaCPRincluding
a second-harmonic term arises naturally [32]. More recently, the
second-harmonic form of CPR has been explored in the context
of JTWPA [33]: by tuning the relative weights of the harmonic
CPR components, substantial ampliﬁcation can be obtained,
with gains up to 13 dB even without the implementation of
dispersion engineering. Furthermore, it was discussed how non-
sinusoidal contributions to the CPR can drive the system from
a stable, periodic regime into chaotic dynamics, particularly in
the case of Jc2 < 0. We note that additional circuit embedding

As evident in Fig. 1, where the equivalent electric circuit of the
investigated JTWPA is shown, the transmission line is made by

At the beginning of the line is applied the signal to amplify, I s,
the microwave pump tone, I p and an optional DC bias current
I DC, used to shift the equilibrium phase of the junctions. Z 0
represents the source and load impedances, typically 50 Ω. The
voltage at the Vout port represents the ampliﬁed signal, as well

work we consider a purely current-biased operation and neglect
any externally applied magnetic ﬂux bias, Φ ext = 0, so that the
non-sinusoidal CPR is treated as a junction-level property rather
than a topology-induced effect.
Using the Kirckhoff’s laws and the constitutive relation of
the components, the circuit in Fig. 1 can be easily converted
in a set of nonlinear, coupled ordinary differential equations,
describing the time evolution of voltages and currents in each
part of the circuit. The system of differential equations can
then be solved using standard numerical methods [35]. The
system’s dynamics are obtained by integrating the system of N
coupled differential equations, one for each cell of the JTWPA.
The time-domain integration is performed with an in-house
developed FORTRAN code implementing the implicit ﬁnite-
difference scheme (tridiagonal solver), while FFT-based spectral
post-processing is carried out using the Mathematica [36] soft-
ware. The chosen normalized time step and integration time are
Δt = 0.01 and tmax = 20000, respectively. Numerical details
are reported in [20]. The Josephson nonlinearity is retained in
full through the non-sinusoidal CPR (5), i.e., no small-signal
or Taylor expansion of the nonlinear term is employed. Re-
lated time-domain multiphysics/FDTD–FEM approaches have
recently been reported [37].
The design parameters were chosen to mimic a real device,
designed and realized by INRIM-Italy, and are reported in Ta-
ble I. The JTWPA is biased with a pump tone, with a frequency
of 7 GHz and a power ranging from -70 to -45 dBm, and a small
signal tone, with a power of -100 dBm and frequency ranging
from 4 to 10 GHz. The Fourier spectrum of the output signal at
Vout is analyzed using fast FFT algorithms.

III. JTWPA WITH SECOND HARMONIC CPR
When considering a modiﬁed CPR, like in (5), an additional
parameter is introduced, namely the ratio between the second
and ﬁrst harmonic of the CPR: Jc2/Jc1. This value can range
typically from -1 to 1, where 0 means standard CPR, as in (3).
In performing the numerical simulation of the system and to be
comparable with the pure sinusoidal CPR, for each choice of the
Jc2/Jc1 ratio, we have rescaled the α parameter in (5) in such a
way that I c corresponds to the maximum value of IJ(ϕ).
The effect of second-harmonic on the JTWPA dynam-
ics appears quite destabilizing, as it shifts the threshold of
chaos to lower pump power levels, see Fig. 2(d)–(f). How-
ever, for Jc2/ Jc1 = −0.6, a larger gain is observed for a
pump power of -64 dBm, see Fig. 2(e), thus showing that
the harmonic component of the CPR is helping to achieve
a more efﬁcient energy transfer between the pump and the
signal.
To improve the JTWPA gain, limited by the transmission line
dispersion that causes a dephasing between pump and signal
tones, typically Resonant Phase Matching (RPM) elements are
periodically added to the transmission line [39], [41], [42].
These consist of parallel LC resonators connected to ground and
capacitively coupled to the transmission line each n cells. The
role of the resonators is to change the wavevector of the pump
tone,whenitisclosetotheirresonancefrequency,thusrephasing
it with the signal. It has been numerically and experimentally
demonstrated that, in this way, a gain larger than 20 dB can be
achieved [39], [42]. The question is whether this mechanism
is still valid in presence of non-sinusoidal CPR. To check this
hypothesis, we have implemented the JTWPA model with RPM
elements, tuned at a frequency of 7 GHz. To speed up the
model development, and to check the consistency of different
numerical modeling schemes, we have implemented the RPM
JTWPA using a SPICE schematic simulator: the freely available
LTSPICE [43].
We have deﬁned the Josephson element, which is not present
in the default libraries of LTSPICE, by means of controlled
current sources, a standard SPICE component, and build the

IV. CONCLUSION
Direct numerical simulation of JTWPA dynamics can provide
insight into the device operation, including unwanted effects.
JTWPAs made with Josephson junctions having non-standard
CPR show signiﬁcant changes in the operative parameters, such
as maximum gain and chaos transition threshold. The implemen-
tation of Resonant Phase Matching circuits improves the JTWPA
signal gain also in the case of nonstandard current proﬁles.
However, care must be taken to avoid excessive generations of
spurious signals. We emphasize that the present time-domain
model is classical and deterministic: the increased spectral
‘noise’ observed in Fig. 4 reﬂects nonlinear mixing and/or
intermodulation products, while a quantitative assessment of
the added (quantum) noise requires a quantum input–output
treatment [44] and related JTWPA quantum-noise analyses [45].

The phase dynamics of Josephson junctions (JJs) under external electromagnetic radiation is
studied through numerical simulations. Current-voltage characteristics, Lyapunov exponents, and
Poincare sections are analyzed in detail. It is found that the subharmonic Shapiro steps at certain
parameters are separated by structured chaotic windows. By performing a linear regression on the
linear part of the data, a fractal dimension of D ¼ 0.868 is obtained, with an uncertainty of 60.012.
The chaotic regions exhibit scaling similarity, and it is shown that the devil’s staircase of the sys-
tem can form a backbone that uniﬁes and explains the highly correlated and structured chaotic
behavior. These features suggest a system possessing multiple complete devil’s staircases. The
onset of chaos for subharmonic steps occurs through the Feigenbaum period doubling scenario.
Universality in the sequence of periodic windows is also demonstrated. Finally, the inﬂuence of the
radiation and JJ parameters on the structured chaos is investigated, and it is concluded that the
structured chaos is a stable formation over a wide range of parameter values. V

If some parameter of an oscillatory system is varied, and
the interaction between an oscillator and its driver is
strong enough, the oscillator can resonate at, or “lock”
onto, an inﬁnity of driving frequencies, giving rise to
steps (the so-called devil’s staircase) with a fractal dimen-
sion between 0 and 1. Phase-locking is an inherent prop-
erty of a large class of oscillatory systems in which the
steps arise as the oscillator passes through regimes that
are phase-locked (and not phased-locked) to the driver.
When system is phase-locked, the ratio between the two
frequencies is a rational number. For weak coupling, the
phase-locked intervals are narrow, so that even if there is
an inﬁnity of intervals, the motion is quasiperiodic for
most driving frequencies; that is, the ratio between the
two frequencies is more likely to be irrational. When the
coupling increases, the phase-locked portions increase,
and it becomes less likely that the motion is quasiperi-
odic. This leads to a unique situation, in which it becomes
important to ask whether a physical quantity is rational
or irrational. In the present work, we numerically investi-
gate a peculiar type of phase-locking that occurs in the
oscillatory system consisting of a single Josephson junc-
tion, driven by external microwave radiation. Over a cer-
tain range of parameters, we observe steps belonging to a
complete devil’s staircase (with fractal dimension close to
0.87) which has been destroyed in a very systematic way.
As the parameter is varied, repeated parts of the stair-
case are destroyed and replaced by self-similar chaotic
windows, which preserve the scaling properties of the
original staircase.
I. INTRODUCTION
Nonlinear dynamical systems like the Josephson junction
(JJ) exhibit a wide variety of chaotic phenomena and are an
interesting ﬁeld of research for both the fundamental and
applied sciences.1,2 Much progress has been made through nu-
merical simulations of many important characteristics of
chaos.3 Investigations of critical exponents in various routes
to chaos, such as period-doubling bifurcations, intermittency,
and quasi-periodicity lend support to the universality and scal-
ing behavior predicted by theoretical models.4 In a Josephson
junction driven by an external microwave radiation, the dev-
il’s staircase structure is realized as a consequence of the
interplay of the Josephson plasma frequency, and the applied
frequency. (See Refs. 5 and 6 and the references therein.)
The devil’s staircase appears in other systems, including
the inﬁnite spin chains with long-range interactions,7 frustrated
quasi-two-dimensional spin-dimer system in magnetic ﬁelds,8
systems of strongly interacting Rydberg atoms,9 and in frac-
tional quantum Hall effect.10 The synchronization of Josephson
and Bloch oscillations results in the quantization of transresist-
ance which also leads to a devil’s staircase structure.11 A dev-
il’s staircase in a spin-torque nano-oscillator driven by a
microwave ﬁeld was experimentally demonstrated in Ref. 12.
In earlier studies of the rf-current-driven JJ, it was found
that, depending on the amplitude of the rf current, the system
would develop a chaotic character.13–16 It was also shown

More recently, the importance of chaos in intrinsic JJs, and

In a further comprehensive study, the critical behavior of
the dynamical equation, in the sense of how it goes from regu-

critical behavior is that of the circle map. Here, in the subcriti-

(i.e., having irrational winding number), whereas in the super-
critical, state the dynamics is composed of chaotic jumps

JJ with its surroundings was considered by coupling it in par-

this case, the chaos develops through the familiar inﬁnite
sequence of period doubling bifurcations.
Other studies exist that try to understand the irregular
response of dissipative systems driven by external sources
when such behavior is interleaved by the synchronized
motion (Shapiro steps). This so called intermittent chaos is
modeled by a random walk between the two neighboring
steps that have become unstable. A simple physical model
was proposed in Ref. 23 and used for an analytic calculation
of the power spectrum of the intermittent-type chaos occur-
ring in rf- and dc-current-driven JJs. It was shown that the
power spectrum of the voltage correlations has a broadband
background characterizing the chaotic solution. A similar
random walk model was developed to explain the phase syn-
chronization of chaotic rotators.24
The microwave-induced devil’s staircase structure and
chaotic behavior in current-fed JJs were studied experimen-
tally and through analog simulations within the resistively
and capacitively shunted junction (RCSJ) model in Ref. 25.
Many externally driven dissipative systems demonstrate the
occurrence of sequences of periodic states separated by gaps
of a chaotic or intermittent nature.23 Different features and
types of intermittent transitions to the chaotic state were
investigated in Refs. 23 and 26–29. The RCSJ model was
used to study the onset of chaotic behavior in the over-
damped JJ, where a transition from unlocked quasiperiodic
motion via subharmonic locked steps to the chaotic region
occurs.5,30 In dynamical systems, intermittency is the tempo-
